plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: A triangular integration region must be split into two Type-I subregions because the lower boundary is y = -x + 1 on the left of the y-axis and y = x + 1 on the right, while horizontal Type-II slices cover the same region without splitting.

interactions.label: Lower boundary equations
interactions.teaches: The two Type-I subintegrals arise because the lower boundary has one formula on the left of x = 0 and a different formula on the right; changing a boundary equation changes the corresponding shaded subregion and its inner limits

interactions.label: Slice type
interactions.teaches: Vertical slices require two x-intervals because the lower y-bound changes formula, while horizontal slices span the region from left edge to right edge with one continuous pair of x-limits

demo_steps.title: Read the boundary formulas
demo_steps.narration: The top of the region is always y = 3, but the lower edge is piecewise: y = -x + 1 for the left half and y = x + 1 for the right half.

demo_steps.title: Why vertical slices split the region
demo_steps.narration: A vertical slice in R1 starts at y = -x + 1 and ends at y = 3, while a vertical slice in R2 starts at y = x + 1 and ends at y = 3. Because the lower limit changes formula at x = 0, the Type-I integral must be written as two integrals.

demo_steps.title: Edit the lower boundaries
demo_steps.narration: Changing either lower-boundary equation redraws that edge and updates the matching shaded region and limits, making clear that the algebraic boundary formula determines the integral bounds.

demo_steps.title: Switch the order of integration
demo_steps.narration: With horizontal slices, each slice runs from the left boundary x = -(y - 1) to the right boundary x = y - 1 for 1 ≤ y ≤ 3, so the whole triangle is covered without splitting.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The need to split a double integral depends on the slicing direction: vertical slices see a piecewise lower boundary, but horizontal slices see one continuous left-to-right span.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D coordinate-plane layout matching the textbook figure: the triangular region is inverted with a horizontal top edge at y = 3, lower vertex on the y-axis at (0, 1), and top corners at x = -2 and x = 2. Draw the triangle outline in thick cyan. Fill R1 with pale blue and R2 with pale yellow, divided by the y-axis. Labels should use italic math styling and be placed near their corresponding edges: y = -x + 1 on the left, y = x + 1 on the right, and y = 3 above the top edge. In Type-I mode, show two red vertical strips and the two separate limit annotations. In Type-II mode, replace them with a blue horizontal strip across the triangle and show the single horizontal-slice limit annotation.
